title: Iran’s Secret Leader Says “I Disagreed” — But Peace Talks Go On
summary: Imagine the most powerful person in your country never shows their face or speaks in public — and when they finally say something, it’s just one sentence. That’s what happened in Iran this week. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei wrote, “I, as a matter of principle, held a different view.” He was talking about a big peace deal with the United States, called a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU). An MoU is like a promise between countries to stop fighting and work things out. Even though he disagreed, Khamenei said he approved the deal because Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, took responsibility for it. On Sunday, top leaders from Iran and the U.S. met in Switzerland. Iran’s parliament speaker and foreign minister were there, and U.S. Vice President JD Vance led the American team. Pakistan and Qatar are helping the two sides talk. The goal is a 60-day roadmap to end a war that started in February. But not everyone in Iran is happy. A TV interview with a hardline cleric who said Khamenei wanted more — like control of a key waterway called the Strait of Hormuz — was cut off after 11 minutes. The TV boss later quit. Some Iranian officials say almost everyone on the security council voted yes, except one ultra-hardliner. The deal is supposed to stop fighting everywhere, including Lebanon. But Iran says Israel is still attacking there, so they closed the strait again — though the U.S. says it’s still open. Now the talks in Switzerland will try to make sure the peace deal actually works.
why_it_matters: When big countries argue and a key oil passage like the Strait of Hormuz gets blocked, it can raise the price of gasoline for your family's car and affect products shipped around the world.

background_read: Iran is a country in the Middle East that has often disagreed with the United States for many years.
The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway where about one-fifth of the world's oil passes through, so keeping it open is important for everyone.
Peace talks like these often take place in neutral countries like Switzerland, where both sides feel safe to meet.
Article_Structure: WHO: Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, President Masoud Pezeshkian, U.S. Vice President JD Vance, and officials from Pakistan and Qatar.
WHAT: Iran and the U.S. are pushing a peace deal (MoU) with a 60-day roadmap, even though the Supreme Leader said he originally disagreed.
WHERE: Peace talks happened in Switzerland; the dispute involves the Strait of Hormuz and fighting in Lebanon.
WHY: The goal is to stop a war that began in February and to bring calm to the whole region, but hardliners in Iran are not happy.

perspectives.description: Supporters of the MoU believe this deal will finally end the fighting and save many lives in the region.
Some powerful people in Iran think the deal is too weak and want more control, like over the Strait of Hormuz, before they accept peace.
Countries like Pakistan and Qatar are helping because they believe talks, even difficult ones, are better than war.
